extracted.intended_audience: readers of 19th-century literary and philosophical prose; students and scholars of Thomas Carlyle
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from Thomas Carlyle's Sartor Resartus presenting autobiographical-philosophical reflections on childhood, education, names, and pedagogy. The text is narrative/essayistic rather than a formal guideline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of Names (right_Naming)
rubrics_metrics.description: Names are among 'the most important of all Clothings' and a 'right_Naming' shapes speech, science, poetry and identity ('Call one a thief, and he will steal').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naming is presented as formative: the act of naming can fix character and destiny. Example: Adam's first task was giving names; a correct name frames perception and subsequent behavior. Anti-pattern: indifferent or careless naming that fails to capture essence and thus misleads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gift a Tool to the Child
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The choicest present you can make him is a Tool; be it knife or pen-gun, for construction or for destruction; either way it is for Work, for Change.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides child development toward activity and a creative instinct ('schaffenden Trieb'). Practical implication: provide implements that encourage making and learning-by-doing. Anti-pattern: gifting passive amusements that do not cultivate workmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children's Play as Training for Cooperation and Roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Gregarious sports train the boy to co-operation (for war or peace) and the girl to domestic providence (preference for dolls).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Play is viewed as an early rehearsal of social functions and skills (cooperation, governance, domestic management). Example: communal games teach working with others. Note: the text frames roles traditionally; this reflects Carlyle's perspective rather than a neutral modern pedagogical prescription.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of Early Culture and Nurture
rubrics_metrics.description: Early culture and favorable influences either nurture a high-towering tree (genius) or produce a doddered dwarf bush; 'it is the duty of all men...to note down with accuracy the characteristic circumstances of their Education.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes documenting and understanding formative influences; early nurture can make or break talent. Practical guidance: carefully observe and record educational circumstances to see what furthers or hinders development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of Passivity and Activity in Education
rubrics_metrics.description: Good Passivity alone is insufficient; education should foster both 'good Passivity and good Activity together' so a child can both receptively learn and actively make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns against overemphasis on passive reception (mere observation) or excessive suppression of active impulse. Suggests curricula/exposure that allow observation and hands-on practice. Anti-pattern: an upbringing that 'hems in' active power and stifles initiative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obedience as Foundational but Tempered
rubrics_metrics.description: Obedience is called 'our universal duty and destiny' and early training in obedience lays the basis of worldly discretion and morality, though excessive spiritual pride should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positions obedience as necessary for social functioning and moral growth, while implying it should be coupled with other virtues (not leading to spiritual pride). Practical tension: cultivate discipline without crushing individuality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of Rote Schooling and Dead Vocables
rubrics_metrics.description: Schooling that 'crammed' innumerable 'dead Vocables' and treated Memory plus birch-rods as instruction is condemned; real fostering of mind requires living thought, not mechanical etymology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers should kindle living thought in students; mere grammatical drilling or punitive discipline is inadequate. Example anti-patterns: mechanical Gerund-grinder teachers, instruction reduced to memorization with corporal punishment. Recommendation: prioritize teachers who demonstrate and inspire thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevate and Honor the Profession of Teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Argues that communities should recognize teaching on par with other high callings (analogous to Generals/Field‑marshals), giving dignity and status to those who 'fashion the souls of a generation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls for social and institutional recognition of teaching's importance. Practical implication: invest in and honor educators so they can attract talent and effect cultural change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposure to the Wider World as Formative
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiences such as the Postwagen, swallows' migration, and the annual Cattle-fair expand imagination and historical sense; these worldly sights form an 'Alphabet' for reading the Volume of the World.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommends broad sensory and social experiences (travel, fairs, interaction with craftsmen and travelers) to stimulate curiosity, historical perspective, and imaginative growth. Anti-pattern: overly secluded upbringing that denies contact with diverse sights and people.
